title: Blockchain Architecture & Enterprise Solutions
tagline: When blockchain fits, how to design permissioned networks, scale, connect, protect data and decide like an architect
summary: A senior-level course on blockchain in organisations: an honest test of when a ledger is the right tool, permissioned and consortium networks with endorsement, chaincode and multi-organisation approvals, scalability with rollups, channels and anchoring, interoperability with atomic swaps and bridges, privacy, consent, key management and consortium governance, and architecture decision records, requirements, risk and staged delivery. Solidity and JavaScript listings were checked. This course teaches architecture judgement; it is not legal advice and names platforms only as examples.

modules.title: When blockchain fits the enterprise
modules.summary: An honest decision test, the alternatives, stakeholders and total cost of ownership.
modules.outcome: You can test whether blockchain suits a use case, compare it with alternatives and estimate costs honestly.
modules.intro: Many enterprise blockchain pilots ended without reaching production, and a common reason was that a shared database would have done the job. Senior architects are valued for saying 'no' when it is the right answer. This module teaches the decision test and the cost thinking behind it.

topics.title: An honest decision test
topics.html:
The classic test, with comments
QuestionIf the answer is no
Do you need shared state across organisations?A normal database owned by one organisation will do
Do the parties have conflicting interests?Standard integration may be enough
Is there no trusted central party?Let the trusted party operate the database
Do you need a verifiable, ordered history?Logs and backups may be enough
Do you really need to avoid reconciliation?Better data exchange standards may solve it

The test is deliberately demanding. The cases that pass are real, but fewer than the enthusiasm of the last decade suggested: supply chains with competing parties, consortium settlement, shared registries without a central owner. Many problems blamed on 'lack of blockchain' were really lack of data standards, incentives or governance.

Check what you just learned

1. Which signal most strongly suggests a ledger may help?
  • A single company wants faster reports
  • The marketing team likes the idea
  • Several parties who do not trust one another need a shared, tamper-evident record with no neutral operator (correct)
  • The data is private to one team

Distrust among parties with no neutral operator.

Check what you just learned

1. If one trusted party can run the database, you should:
  • Avoid technology
  • Always use blockchain
  • Build a token
  • Use a database (correct)

Simpler and cheaper.
keyPoints: Use a structured test: shared writes, distrust, no neutral operator, tamper evidence.
Fewer problems need a ledger than hype suggested.

topics.title: Alternatives to consider first
topics.html:
Options on the table
OptionStrengthWeakness
Shared database run by one partyCheap, fast, simpleOthers must trust the operator
Standard APIs and data formatsFixes reconciliation without new infrastructureNo tamper evidence across parties
Event streaming platformHigh throughput and ordered logsStill run by an operator
Notarisation: hashes anchored on a public chainCheap proof that a record existed, without revealing itDoes not manage shared state
Permissioned consortium ledgerShared state, signed changes, no single operatorCost, complexity and governance
Public blockchainOpen verification and censorship resistancePublic data, variable cost and limited privacy

Questions to ask each stakeholder

  1. What exactly goes wrong today, and what does it cost?
  2. Who would run the system, and who would worry about that?
  3. What data may never be shared, and with whom?
  4. Which laws and standards apply?
  5. What would make you leave the network?
  6. How will we know the pilot succeeded?

Check what you just learned

1. Why look at standard APIs before a ledger?
  • Many reconciliation problems are caused by inconsistent data formats, which a ledger does not fix (correct)
  • APIs are fashionable
  • Ledgers cannot use APIs
  • APIs are always cheaper

Fix the real cause.

Check what you just learned

1. Notarisation proves:
  • That the record is true
  • That a record existed at a time (correct)
  • Who owns it
  • That it is private

Existence and integrity only.
keyPoints: Compare with databases, APIs, streams and notarisation before choosing a ledger.
Ask each stakeholder what exactly goes wrong today.

topics.title: Cost, value and honest business cases
topics.html:
Total cost comparison

Change setup, running costs and the yearly reconciliation cost avoided to compare a consortium ledger with a shared database. A teaching model with made-up figures (rupees).

Adjust Extra setup for the ledger, Extra yearly running cost for the ledger, Yearly reconciliation cost avoided, Years and see Net extra cost of the ledger over the period change.

Costs that business cases forget
CostWhy it matters
Governance and legal set-upAgreeing rules among organisations takes months
Integration with existing systemsOften larger than the ledger itself
Operations skills and on-call supportEach member must run infrastructure
Key management and securityHardware, procedures and audits
Change managementPeople must use the new process
Exit and wind-downEvery network needs a plan for the end

Common mistakes

  • Counting only the benefits of the technology and ignoring governance cost.
  • Running a pilot with no success measures.
  • Treating a successful demo as proof of a viable network.

Check what you just learned

1. Why define success measures before a pilot?
  • For marketing
  • Auditors require it
  • Without them nobody can decide honestly whether to continue (correct)
  • They lower cost

Decide with evidence.

Check what you just learned

1. A pilot without success measures produces:
  • Standards
  • Savings
  • Certainty
  • Opinions, not evidence (correct)

Hard to decide.

Key terms: flip and sort

Permissioned network
A network where members are known and approved
Consortium
A group of organisations sharing a network
Notarisation
Anchoring a hash to prove existence
Reconciliation
Making two records agree
TCO
Total cost of ownership
Pilot
A limited trial with success measures
keyPoints: Count governance, integration, operations and exit costs.
Define success measures before a pilot.

modules.title: Permissioned and consortium networks
modules.summary: Known members, endorsement, consensus choices, chaincode and on-chain approvals among organisations.
modules.outcome: You can describe how permissioned networks work, read chaincode and design multi-organisation approvals.
modules.intro: When the parties are known companies, the design choices change. You do not need anonymous strangers to validate transactions; you need the right organisations to endorse them. This module explains the platforms, the consensus options and the way approvals are modelled.

topics.title: How permissioned platforms work
topics.html:
Typical platforms (examples, not recommendations)
PlatformStyleNotable ideas
Hyperledger FabricModular; chaincode in Go, JavaScript or JavaChannels for private data; endorsement policies; separate ordering service
Hyperledger BesuEthereum-compatible permissioned or public clientSolidity smart contracts; QBFT or IBFT consensus; privacy options
CordaPeer-to-peer ledgers shared only between parties to a dealContracts in JVM languages; notary services
Definition

Endorsement policy. A rule stating which organisations must sign a transaction for it to be valid, for example 'at least two of the four members' or 'customs must always sign'.

Check what you just learned

1. What does an endorsement policy decide?
  • Which organisations must sign a transaction for it to be valid (correct)
  • The price of gas
  • The block size
  • The programming language

Business rules about agreement.

Check what you just learned

1. Channels in Fabric let:
  • Anyone read everything
  • A subset of members share private data (correct)
  • Gas fall
  • Blocks grow

Need-to-know separation.
keyPoints: Permissioned platforms use known members, endorsement and an ordering service.
Different platforms make different trade-offs.

topics.title: Chaincode: business rules on a shared ledger
topics.html:
What the chaincode shows
FeatureReason
Existence check before creatingPrevents overwriting a record
Allowed status listRejects invalid states
Organisation identity from the transaction contextRecords and checks who acted
Only customs may clear a shipmentA role rule in the application
History array with identity and timeA tamper-evident audit trail
Deterministic code onlyEvery endorsing peer must compute the same result
Watch out

Chaincode must be deterministic. Using random numbers, local time or external calls can make endorsing peers disagree and reject the transaction.

Check what you just learned

1. Why must chaincode be deterministic?
  • It is faster
  • Judges require it
  • Different peers run it and must reach the same result (correct)
  • It uses less memory

Agreement depends on identical results.

Check what you just learned

1. The organisation making a call is available from:
  • A comment
  • A global variable
  • The browser
  • The transaction context (correct)

Client identity.
keyPoints: Chaincode implements business rules and uses the caller's organisation identity.
It must be deterministic.

topics.title: Consensus and approvals among organisations
topics.html:
Consensus in permissioned settings
ApproachIdeaTolerates
Raft (crash fault tolerant)A leader orders transactions; followers replicateMachines that stop, but not machines that lie
IBFT / QBFT (Byzantine fault tolerant)Validators vote in rounds and need two thirds agreementUp to a third of validators misbehaving
Proof of authorityNamed validators take turnsDepends on honest authorities

The right choice depends on trust. Members of a consortium who trust each other not to lie, but fear crashes, may choose Raft. Members who worry that one participant might act maliciously need a Byzantine fault tolerant algorithm, which tolerates fewer failures per validator but costs more messages.

What the approval contract adds
FeatureReason
Quorum of different organisationsNo single organisation can decide alone
One approval per member per proposalNo double counting
DeadlineProposals do not stay open forever
Hash of the proposal textThe decision is tied to an exact document
EventsMonitoring and audit

Check what you just learned

1. Which consensus fits members who fear a malicious participant?
  • A Byzantine fault tolerant algorithm such as QBFT (correct)
  • Raft
  • A random draw
  • A single leader forever

Raft assumes participants do not lie.

Check what you just learned

1. A quorum of different organisations prevents:
  • All fees
  • One member deciding alone (correct)
  • All delays
  • All disputes

Shared control.

Key terms: flip and sort

Endorsement
A signature by an organisation that approves a transaction
Chaincode
Smart contract code on Fabric
Channel
A private sub-ledger among some members
Ordering service
The component that sequences transactions
Raft
A crash-fault-tolerant consensus algorithm
QBFT
A Byzantine-fault-tolerant consensus algorithm
keyPoints: Choose Raft for crashes and BFT algorithms for possible malice.
Record multi-organisation approvals with quorums and deadlines.

modules.title: Scalability and performance
modules.summary: Throughput limits, rollups, channels, sidechains and anchoring, with simple numbers to compare them.
modules.outcome: You can explain the scaling techniques, estimate throughput and choose an approach for a given need.
modules.intro: Scalability is a trade between speed, cost, security and decentralisation. Enterprise needs are usually modest compared with public networks, which changes the answer. This module explains the techniques and gives you the arithmetic to judge them.

topics.title: Why chains are slow, and what you can do
topics.html:
Every node in a public chain processes every transaction, so throughput is limited by what an ordinary computer can verify. Block size or gas limits, block time and the time to spread data all matter. Increasing them helps, but makes it harder for ordinary participants to run nodes, which weakens decentralisation. This is the heart of the scalability trade-off.

Options and what they trade
OptionHow it scalesWhat you give up
Larger blocks or faster blocksMore data per second on the base chainFewer people can run nodes
RollupsExecute off-chain, post compressed data and proofs on the base chainMore complex systems, withdrawal delays or proving cost
State channelsParties exchange signed updates off-chain, settle only at the endOnly for a fixed set of participants
SidechainsA separate chain with its own validatorsWeaker security than the base chain
Permissioned networksFewer, known validators agree quicklyLess decentralisation by design
Batching and anchoringPublish only a hash of many recordsRecords live elsewhere

Check what you just learned

1. Why not simply make blocks huge?
  • It is illegal
  • Blocks cannot grow
  • Fewer participants could run nodes, weakening decentralisation (correct)
  • Fees would be zero

Scalability is a trade-off.

Check what you just learned

1. State channels suit:
  • Voting
  • Anonymous crowds
  • One-off payments
  • A fixed group exchanging many updates (correct)

Fixed participants.
keyPoints: Throughput is limited by what nodes can verify.
Every scaling option trades something away.

topics.title: Rollups explained with numbers
topics.html:
Optimistic versus zero-knowledge
Optimistic rollupZero-knowledge rollup
How correctness is ensuredAssume correct; challenge if fraud is shownProve correct with a validity proof
Withdrawal to the base chainWait for the challenge periodAs soon as the proof is verified
Computation costLowerHigher to generate proofs
Maturity of toolsLonger track recordRapidly improving

Throughput estimator

Change the block gas limit and per-transaction gas to compare plain transfers on the base chain with compressed rollup data. A teaching model.

Adjust Block gas limit, Gas per plain transfer, Gas per rollup transaction, Seconds per block and see Plain transfers per second, Rollup transactions per second change.

Check what you just learned

1. What posting does a rollup need on the base chain?
  • Compressed transaction data and a state summary or proof (correct)
  • Nothing at all
  • Private keys
  • Full node software

That is how the base chain keeps the final say.

Check what you just learned

1. Optimistic rollups rely on:
  • Validity proofs
  • Fraud proofs (correct)
  • Private keys
  • Trust in one operator forever

A challenge window.
keyPoints: Rollups execute off-chain and post compressed data to the base chain.
Optimistic rollups wait for challenges; zero-knowledge rollups use proofs.

topics.title: Choosing for enterprise needs
topics.html:
Typical enterprise numbers
Use caseRough scaleImplication
Cross-organisation shipment eventsTens to thousands of events per minuteA permissioned network is more than enough
Document anchoringMillions of records per day, one root per batchBatching makes throughput irrelevant
Consumer micro-paymentsMany tiny transfersA rollup or off-chain scheme may be needed
High-frequency tradingThousands per second with microsecond latencyA blockchain is the wrong tool

Anchoring rules

  1. Hash each record twice or with a type prefix to avoid confusing leaves and inner nodes.
  2. Keep the records and the proofs in your own system.
  3. Use a dedicated low-balance key with only the anchorer role.
  4. Wait for confirmations before telling anyone a batch is anchored.
  5. Test a proof end to end before you rely on it.

Check what you just learned

1. Why is throughput rarely a problem for anchoring?
  • Chains are infinitely fast
  • Records are free
  • Only one small root is posted per batch, however many records it covers (correct)
  • Roots are not hashes

One transaction covers millions of records.

Check what you just learned

1. A Merkle proof shows:
  • The price
  • The record is true
  • Who owns it
  • A record was part of an anchored batch (correct)

Inclusion only.

Key terms: flip and sort

Throughput
Transactions per second
Rollup
Off-chain execution with data posted on-chain
Sequencer
The party ordering rollup transactions
State channel
Off-chain exchange between fixed parties
Sidechain
A separate chain with its own security
Anchoring
Publishing a hash that commits to many records
keyPoints: Most enterprise use cases need modest throughput.
Anchoring a Merkle root scales to any number of records.

modules.title: Interoperability and cross-chain communication
modules.summary: Atomic swaps, bridges, messaging and the trust assumptions of each.
modules.outcome: You can explain how chains communicate, build and read an HTLC and judge a bridge design by its trust assumptions.
modules.intro: Real systems rarely live on one chain. Assets, messages and proofs need to cross boundaries, and each crossing is a place where trust assumptions hide. This module explains the main approaches and why bridges have been so heavily attacked.

topics.title: Atomic swaps and hashed time-locks
topics.html:
Why the deadlines differ
PointReason
Bob's lock is shorter than Alice'sAlice reveals the secret on chain B; Bob must still have time to use it on chain A
A margin between the twoAbsorbs delays and congestion
Refund only after the deadlineNobody can take funds back early
The secret is public once revealedIt can never be reused for another swap

Check what you just learned

1. Why is the second lock shorter than the first?
  • The first party reveals the secret on the second chain, and the second party still needs time to claim on the first (correct)
  • To save gas
  • It is random
  • It is required by sha256

Safe ordering of deadlines.

Check what you just learned

1. After a claim, the secret is:
  • Private
  • Public on that chain (correct)
  • Deleted
  • Encrypted

That lets the other side claim.
keyPoints: Hashed time-locks make swaps trust-minimised: claim with the secret or refund after the deadline.
Deadlines must leave a safe margin.

topics.title: Bridges and why they fail
topics.html:
Kinds of bridge
KindHow it worksTrust assumption
Lock and mintLock assets on chain A, mint wrapped copies on chain BThe locking contract and the party attesting to deposits
Burn and releaseBurn wrapped copies, release the originalsThe same
Liquidity networkProviders hold funds on both sides and swapThe providers' honesty and capital
Light-client bridgeChain B verifies chain A's consensus directlyCryptography and the security of both chains
Messaging layerRelayers carry signed messages between chainsThe relayer set or oracle network

Bridges concentrate enormous value in one place and depend on complex code and small sets of keys. They have been among the most attacked systems in the field. A bridge is only as secure as its weakest link: the contract on either side, the verification, the keys of the attesters or the upgrade authority.

Defensive design

  1. Prefer verification by cryptography over trust in a few operators.
  2. Limit the value that can pass in a given period.
  3. Add monitoring and the ability to pause.
  4. Protect upgrade authority with multi-signature control and a time-lock.
  5. Use separate audits for each chain's contracts and the off-chain components.
  6. Plan how users are made whole if something fails.

Check what you just learned

1. Why are bridges attractive targets?
  • They are slow
  • They are public
  • They hold large pools of assets guarded by complex code and a few keys (correct)
  • They have no contracts

A big prize behind a narrow door.

Check what you just learned

1. Rate limits on a bridge:
  • Delay all blocks
  • Raise fees
  • Hide transfers
  • Reduce the damage of a flaw (correct)

Cap the loss.
keyPoints: Bridges move value across chains but concentrate risk.
Prefer cryptographic verification, limits, monitoring and strong upgrade control.

topics.title: Messaging, standards and enterprise integration
topics.html:
Integration patterns
PatternUseCare
Event listeners and webhooksTell internal systems when something happens on-chainConfirmations, retries and idempotence
OraclesBring outside data on-chainSource quality and manipulation
AnchoringConnect private systems to a public chain by hashOnly proves existence
Cross-chain messaging protocolsSend instructions between chainsTrust in relayers and verification
Standard token and identity formatsMake assets and credentials portableGovernance of the standard

Enterprise checklist for interoperability

  1. Which systems must exchange data, and in which direction?
  2. Which standards do the partners already use?
  3. What happens if the other side is down or compromised?
  4. Who is liable for cross-system failures?
  5. How are keys and secrets shared safely?
  6. What is the exit plan if a connector is retired?

Timelock margin

Change the two timelocks and the margin needed to see whether the swap leaves a safe gap. A teaching tool.

Adjust First lock (hours), Second lock (hours), Margin needed (hours) and see Margin between locks (hours), Spare margin (hours) change.

Check what you just learned

1. Why make integration steps idempotent?
  • Messages are retried and may arrive more than once (correct)
  • It is fashionable
  • Chains require it
  • To save gas

Repeats must be harmless.

Check what you just learned

1. Oracle risk comes from:
  • Block size
  • Source quality and manipulation (correct)
  • Gas price
  • Colour

Garbage in, garbage out.

Key terms: flip and sort

Atomic swap
An exchange that either completes for both or for neither
HTLC
Hashed time-lock contract
Bridge
A system moving assets or messages across chains
Wrapped asset
A token representing an asset on another chain
Relayer
A party carrying messages between chains
Light client
A verifier of another chain's consensus
keyPoints: Use events, oracles, anchoring and messaging with idempotence.
Plan for the other side failing and for exit.

modules.title: Privacy, governance and compliance
modules.summary: Data minimisation on immutable ledgers, consent, auditability, key management and consortium governance.
modules.outcome: You can design a ledger that respects data protection, record consent, protect keys and set up governance.
modules.intro: The hardest enterprise questions are not technical. They are: who may see this, who decides, what the law requires and what happens when people disagree. This module covers privacy and compliance design, and the human structures that make a consortium work.

topics.title: Privacy on a ledger that cannot forget
topics.html:
Data-protection laws often give people rights to correct and erase data about them. A shared ledger is designed so that history cannot be rewritten. The conflict is real, and the safest resolution is to keep personal data out of the ledger altogether. Store it where it can be corrected and deleted, and put on the ledger only what is needed for shared agreement: pseudonymous identifiers, hashes, permissions and status.

Data minimisation patterns
PatternHow it worksLimit
Hash on-chain, data off-chainThe ledger holds a fingerprint; the data lives in a protected storeHashes of low-entropy data can be guessed; add random salt
Pseudonymous identifiersA random identifier links ledger entries to a person in a private tableLinkage risk if the table leaks
Private channels or private transactionsOnly parties to a deal see its termsStill visible to those parties and operators
Encryption with managed keysData on-chain is encryptedLaw may still treat it as personal data; keys must last as long as the data
Zero-knowledge proofsProve a fact (for example 'over 18') without revealing the dataSpecialised and complex

Check what you just learned

1. What is the safest way to respect erasure rights on a ledger?
  • Encrypt everything on-chain
  • Delete blocks
  • Keep personal data off the ledger and store only hashes or pseudonymous identifiers (correct)
  • Ignore the law

Design the conflict away.

Watch out

This is not legal advice. Data-protection law differs by country, so involve counsel early.

Check what you just learned

1. Hashing a phone number without salt is risky because:
  • It is free
  • Hashes are slow
  • Hashes are long
  • It can be guessed by trying all numbers (correct)

Low-entropy inputs.
keyPoints: Keep personal data off the ledger; store hashes, pseudonyms and permissions.
Add salt to hashes of guessable data.

topics.title: Consent, audit and identity
topics.html:
What the registry does
FeatureWhy
Hashes of purposes, not textThe record shows what kind of use without revealing details
Per recipient and purposeConsent is specific, not blanket
ExpiryConsent should not last forever by accident
Revoke by the subjectPeople can withdraw
isAllowed is a free view callData holders can check before sharing
Events for grant and revokeAn audit trail

Audit and accountability

  • Log who accessed which record, when and for what purpose.
  • Keep logs tamper-evident, for example by anchoring them.
  • Separate the duties of those who operate systems and those who review them.
  • Test restore and recovery, not only backups.
  • Prepare for regulators' questions in advance.

Check what you just learned

1. Why make consent specific to a purpose?
  • Blanket consent is not meaningful and rarely lawful (correct)
  • Gas is lower
  • Hashes need it
  • Contracts require it

Informed and specific.

Check what you just learned

1. Data holders should call isAllowed:
  • After releasing data
  • Before releasing data (correct)
  • Never
  • Once a year

Check first.
keyPoints: A consent register stores who agreed to what, as hashes and timestamps.
Audit trails should be tamper-evident and reviewed.

topics.title: Keys, roles and consortium governance
topics.html:
Key management at enterprise scale
PracticeReason
Hardware security modules for signing keysKeys cannot be copied out
Separate keys per role and environmentA leak has limited reach
Multi-person approval for sensitive actionsNo single insider can act alone
Rotation and revocation procedures, testedYou will need them one day
Backup and recovery with split custodyLoss must not be fatal
Logs of every use of a keyDetect misuse
Questions a governance charter answers
QuestionTypical answer
Who may join and on what conditions?Approved by a majority, bound by an agreement and technical standards
How are changes approved?Quorum rules, with higher thresholds for the rules themselves
How are costs shared?Equal shares or by usage, agreed yearly
How are disputes settled?Escalation to mediation, then courts, using the ledger as evidence
How does a member leave or get removed?Notice, key revocation, data export and a wind-down plan
Who is liable when something fails?Defined in the agreement, not left to chance

Common mistakes

  • Building the network before agreeing the governance.
  • Letting one member control the ordering service or the keys.
  • Forgetting an exit plan until a member wants to leave.

Check what you just learned

1. Why agree governance before building?
  • It is traditional
  • Auditors demand it
  • Technical choices depend on who decides and who pays, and late disagreement can end the project (correct)
  • It lowers gas

People problems sink more networks than technology.

Check what you just learned

1. A governance charter should include:
  • Nothing
  • A logo
  • A token
  • How members leave (correct)

Every consortium needs an agreed exit plan.

Key terms: flip and sort

Data minimisation
Collecting and storing only what is needed
Pseudonym
An identifier that does not directly name a person
Consent register
A record of agreements to share data
HSM
A hardware security module for keys
Governance
How a group makes and enforces decisions
Charter
The written rules of a consortium
keyPoints: Use hardware-protected keys, separate roles and multi-person approval.
Agree governance, costs, disputes and exit before building.

modules.title: Architectural decision-making
modules.summary: Decision records, non-functional requirements, reference architectures, vendor evaluation, risk registers and the road from pilot to production.
modules.outcome: You can write a decision record, set requirements, evaluate options and plan a pilot honestly.
modules.intro: Architecture is the discipline of making important decisions on purpose, writing down why, and being able to change them later. This module gives you the tools senior architects use, and applies them to a blockchain project.

topics.title: Decision records
topics.html:
The parts of a good decision record
PartPurpose
ContextWhat forces are at work: the problem, constraints, people
Options consideredReal alternatives, including doing nothing
DecisionWhat was chosen, in one clear sentence
ConsequencesGood and bad results, honestly
Status and dateProposed, accepted or superseded
Review triggerWhen to revisit

Habits

  1. Write the record when the decision is made, not months later.
  2. Keep each record short, one page at most.
  3. Store records with the code and review them like code.
  4. Never delete an old decision; mark it superseded.
  5. Record rejected options, because they will be proposed again.

Check what you just learned

1. Why record rejected options?
  • They will be suggested again, and the reasons for rejecting them save a repeat argument (correct)
  • To fill space
  • Auditors require it
  • It is a rule of Git

Institutional memory.

Check what you just learned

1. An ADR should be written:
  • Years later
  • When the decision is made (correct)
  • Never
  • By a vendor

Context is fresh.
keyPoints: A decision record states context, options, decision, consequences and review trigger.
Keep records short, versioned and honest.

topics.title: Requirements, reference architecture and risks
topics.html:
Non-functional requirements to pin down
AreaExample question
PerformanceHow many transactions per minute at peak, and how fast must each be final?
AvailabilityWhat downtime is acceptable? Which parts can degrade gracefully?
SecurityWhich threats matter? Who holds which keys?
Privacy and complianceWhich laws apply and what data is involved?
OperabilityWho runs it, monitors it and is on call?
EvolvabilityHow will we upgrade contracts, rules and members?
CostWhat is the budget for build and for a year of operation?

Risk score

Change likelihood and impact (1 to 5) to see a risk rating. A teaching model.

Adjust Likelihood, Impact and see Score change.

Check what you just learned

1. Why define non-functional requirements early?
  • They are optional
  • Auditors prefer them
  • They shape the architecture; discovering them late is costly (correct)
  • They reduce code

Qualities decide structure.

Check what you just learned

1. A risk score multiplies:
  • Users and nodes
  • Cost and time
  • Gas and price
  • Likelihood and impact (correct)

A simple ranking.
keyPoints: Pin down performance, availability, security, privacy, operability, evolvability and cost.
Use a layered reference architecture and a scored risk register.

topics.title: From pilot to production, and when to stop
topics.html:
A staged path
StageGoalExit test
DiscoveryUnderstand the problem and the alternativesA clear decision: proceed, change approach or stop
Proof of conceptShow that the key technical idea worksWorks end to end with realistic data
PilotRun with real partners on a limited scopeSuccess measures met: cost, time, disputes
ProductionOperate with service levels and governanceStable for a quarter with no major incidents
ScaleAdd members and use casesGovernance handles growth
RetireWind down or migrate when it no longer fitsData exported, members informed

Vendor and technology evaluation

  1. Who else uses it in production, and at what scale?
  2. How active is the community and the maintenance?
  3. What are the licence and support terms?
  4. How easy is it to leave? Is the data portable?
  5. What does an independent security review say?
  6. What would we lose if the vendor disappeared?

A mature organisation treats stopping as a legitimate result. A pilot that shows the problem is better solved with a shared database has succeeded: it saved the cost of a larger mistake. Celebrate that, write it down, and share the lessons.

Check what you just learned

1. When is a pilot successful?
  • When it gives an honest answer to whether to continue, change or stop (correct)
  • When it ends with a press release
  • When it uses the newest technology
  • When it is the cheapest

Evidence beats enthusiasm.

Watch out

Education only. Real enterprise projects need legal, security and compliance review.

Check what you just learned

1. Evaluating a vendor includes asking:
  • Only the price
  • How easy it is to leave (correct)
  • Only the logo
  • Nothing

Avoid lock-in.

Key terms: flip and sort

ADR
Architecture decision record
NFR
Non-functional requirement
Reference architecture
A standard layered design
Risk register
A scored list of risks
Proof of concept
A small build showing an idea works
Lock-in
Difficulty of leaving a vendor or technology
keyPoints: Move from discovery to proof of concept, pilot, production and, if needed, retirement.
Stopping is a legitimate and valuable outcome.
